title: Incompressibility and Spectral Gaps of Random Circuits
authors: Chi-Fang Chen (California Institute of Technology, USA), Jeongwan Haah (Microsoft Quantum, USA), Jonas Haferkamp (Harvard University, USA), Yunchao Liu (University of California, Berkeley, USA), Tony Metger (ETH Zurich, Switzerland), Xinyu Tan (Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA)
abstract: Random reversible and quantum circuits form random walks on the alternating group $\mathrm{Alt}(2^n)$ and unitary group $\mathrm{SU}(2^n)$, respectively, with each random gate as one step of the walk. Existing bounds on the spectral gap for the $t$-th moment of these random walks have inverse-polynomial dependence in both $n$ and $t$. We prove that the gap for random reversible circuits is $\Omega(n^{-3})$ for all $t\geq 1$, and the gap for random quantum circuits is $\Omega(n^{-3})$ for $t \leq \Theta(2^{n/2})$. Importantly, these gaps are independent of $t$ in the respective regimes. We can further improve both gaps to $n^{-1}/\mathrm{polylog}(n, t)$ for $t\leq 2^{\Theta(n)}$, which is tight up to polylog factors in $n$ and $t$. Our spectral gap results have a number of consequences: (1) Random reversible circuits with $O(n^4 t)$ gates form multiplicative-error $t$-wise independent (even) permutations for all $t\geq 1$; for $t \leq \Theta(2^{n/6.1})$, we show that $\tilde O(n^2 t)$ gates suffice. (2) Random quantum circuits with $O(n^4 t)$ gates form multiplicative-error unitary $t$-designs for $t \leq \Theta(2^{n/2})$; for $t\leq \Theta(2^{2n/5})$, we show that $\tilde O(n^2t)$ gates suffice. (3) The robust quantum circuit complexity of random quantum circuits grows linearly for an exponentially long time, proving the robust Brown-Susskind conjecture [BS18, BCHJ+21]. We also show an analogous result for random reversible circuits. Our spectral gap bounds are proven by reducing random quantum circuits to a more structured walk: a modification of the "PFC ensemble" from [MPSY24] together with an expander on the alternating group due to Kassabov [Kas07a], for which we give an efficient implementation using reversible circuits. In our reduction, we approximate the structured walk with local random circuits without losing the gap, which uses tools from the study of frustration-free Hamiltonians.

Abstract—Random reversible and quantum circuits form random walks on the alternating group Alt(2n ) and unitary group
SU(2n ), respectively, with each random gate as one step of the
walk. Existing bounds on the spectral gap for the t-th moment of
these random walks have inverse-polynomial dependence in both
n and t. We prove that the gap for random reversible circuits is
Ω(n−3 ) for all t ≥ 1, and the gap for random quantum circuits is
Ω(n−3 ) for t ≤ Θ(2n/2 ). Importantly, these gaps are independent
of t in the respective regimes. We can further improve both gaps
to n−1 /polylog(n, t) for t ≤ 2Θ(n) , which is tight up to polylog
factors in n and t. Our spectral gap results have a number of
consequences:
1) Random reversible circuits with O(n4 t) gates form
multiplicative-error t-wise independent (even) permutations for all t ≥ 1; for t ≤ Θ(2n/6.1 ), we show that Õ(n2 t)
gates suffice.
2) Random quantum circuits with O(n4 t) gates form
multiplicative-error unitary t-designs for t ≤ Θ(2n/2 ); for
t ≤ Θ(22n/5 ), we show that Õ(n2 t) gates suffice.
3) The robust quantum circuit complexity of random quantum circuits grows linearly for an exponentially long time,
proving the robust Brown–Susskind conjecture [1], [2].
We also show an analogous result for random reversible
circuits.
Our spectral gap bounds are proven by reducing random
quantum circuits to a more structured walk: a modification
of the “PFC ensemble” from [3] together with an expander
on the alternating group due to Kassabov [4], for which we
give an efficient implementation using reversible circuits. In our
reduction, we approximate the structured walk with local random
circuits without losing the gap, which uses tools from the study
of frustration-free Hamiltonians.
Index Terms—unitary t-designs, t-wise independent permutations, random quantum circuits.

A random quantum (or reversible) circuit on n qubits
(or bits) with L gates cannot be implemented by
any quantum (or reversible) circuit with less than
L/ poly(n) gates as long as L ≤ 2Θ(n) .
In other words, the complexity of a random circuit with a fixed
number of qubits grows linearly with the number of random
gates for an exponentially long time, which means that random
circuits are essentially incompressible, resolving a conjecture
of [1], [2].
This linear complexity growth follows from our analysis of
the probability distribution of unitaries (or reversible functions,
i.e., permutations) produced by random circuits. We give
bounds on how quickly this distribution converges to the
uniform distribution on the unitary group on n qubits or the alternating group on n-bit strings as the random circuit deepens.
This convergence to the uniform measures has been studied for
various reasons and often goes under the name of t-designs or
t-wise independence. A unitary or permutation t-design1 is a
distribution whose t-th moments are (almost) the same as those
of the uniform measure. Although the true uniform measures
are hard to sample from, there are efficiently implementable
t-designs, and many randomized algorithms rely on this efficiency. Applications include randomized benchmarking [6],
[7], classical shadows [8], and derandomization [9]. Beyond

I. I NTRODUCTION
Among all Boolean functions on n-bit strings, the vast
majority has exponential circuit complexity. This is based
on a counting argument by Shannon from the 1940’s [5],
and is often summarized by saying that a random function
is complex. A similar argument carries over to the quantum
setting, showing that a Haar random unitary is complex.
Since a sufficiently deep random circuit should produce a

these applications, it is desirable to know higher moments, and

Our main technical result proves that the t-th moment
operator of the random walk produced by random circuits has
a spectral gap of ∆ = Ω(1/ poly(n)) independent of t. This
has been a long-standing open question in the study of random
circuits and is known to imply that random circuits of depth
O(t poly(n)) form t-designs.
The key conceptual insight for our proof is a new globalto-local strategy for analyzing random circuits. Prior work
typically attempted to understand the random walk behavior
of random circuits directly using tools from the Markov
chain literature, but understanding the emergence of global
randomness directly from the local randomness produced
by random circuits proved challenging. We overcome this
by first focussing on highly structured ensembles of global
permutations or unitaries with good mixing properties. Even
though both random circuits and uniformly random permutations/unitaries are structureless, these structured ensembles
of permutations/unitaries allow us to connect the two: On the
one hand, the mixing properties of the structured ensembles
allow us to relate them to uniform randomness; on the other
hand, finding explicit circuit implementations for the structured ensembles allows us to relate them (through a series of
transformations) to random circuits.
For classical permutations, these structured ensembles of
permutations are given by Kassabov’s highly mixing generating set on Alt(2n ) [4]; we show, perhaps surprisingly,
that such a mixing generating set only requires very simple
permutations with short circuit implementations. For unitaries,
we combine our structured ensemble of permutations with the
PFC ensemble from [3], which results, after additional steps, in
a structured ensemble of unitaries with good mixing properties
and efficient circuit implementations. For both the classical
and quantum cases, significant additional work is required to
relate these structured sets to (structureless) random circuits,
which we explain in more detail in Section I-C.

c) Other constructions of t-designs: The gap of random
quantum circuits is used in multiple constructions to prove
the efficient generation of designs for other random processes.
This includes stochastic Hamiltonian dynamics [27], where the
local Hamiltonian randomly fluctuates depending on time [28].
Jian, Bentsen, and Swingle [29] argued that certain random
time-dependent Hamiltonian evolution converges to t-designs
at a linear rate. See also [30], [31]. The gap estimate in [19]
can also be used to show that cluster states randomly measured in the X-Y plane generate approximate t-designs on
the last unmeasured column [32, Appendix]. In particular,
our result improves the scaling in both of these settings to
linear. Previously, the work of Nakata, Hirche, Koashi, and
Winter [33] showed a linear scaling in t for √a family of
stochastic Hamiltonians in the regime t ≤ O( n) without
embedding random quantum circuits.
Recently, structured (rather than locally random) quantum
circuits were used to obtain more efficient t-design constructions. Haah, Liu, and Tan [34] showed that a circuit ensemble
based on “random Pauli rotations” eiθP/2 with a uniformly
random n-qubit Pauli operator P and a uniformly random
angle θ ∈ (−π, π), has a gap of 1/(4t) + 1/(4n − 1) for
all t ≥ 1. This achieves multiplicative-error approximate tdesigns with circuits of depth O(nt2 log n) using all-to-all
gates. Chen, Docter, Xu, Bouland, and Hayden [35] considered
products of two exponentials of random matrix sums, giving
an overall gate complexity Õ(n2 t2 ) for t ≤ 2O(n/ log n) for
approximate t-designs, but only for additive errors, which is
a much weaker notion of approximation that operationally
corresponds to parallel applications of the unitary. Shortly
after, [3], [36] achieved constructions of approximate unitary
t-designs with O(poly(n)t)-depth circuits and additive error
poly(t)/2n . Note that [3], [35], [36] do not show any spectral
gaps for their constructions; nonetheless, the construction
in [3] turns out to be useful for our spectral gap proof of
random quantum circuits, as we explain below.

d) Growth of quantum circuit complexity: Some of the
motivation for a t-independent gap for random circuit stems
from a close connection to quantum circuit complexity: motivated by applications in black hole physics, Brown and
Susskind [1] argued that the circuit complexity (i.e., the size
of the smallest possible circuit that approximately implements
a given unitary) of random quantum circuits should grow at
a linear rate for an exponentially long time because collisions
(circuits accidentally implementing the same unitary) should
be rare. See also Roberts and Yoshida [37]. While intuitive,
this sparsity of collisions seems hard to prove directly.
Towards proving the Brown–Susskind conjecture for random quantum circuits, Haferkamp, Faist, Kothakonda, Eisert,
and Yunger Halpern [38] showed that the exact quantum circuit complexity in random quantum circuits of depth d grows
as Ω(d/poly(n)) until d = 4n /poly(n), when it saturates;
see also Li [39] for two short proofs of this fact. As the name
suggests, the exact circuit complexity counts the number of
gates required to implement a unitary exactly. Unfortunately,
this is too brittle a notion of circuit complexity. A slightly
more robust result for a family of random circuits (using a
non-universal gate set) was obtained in [40], showing a linear
growth up to exponentially small implementation errors in
operator norm, but this is still not an operational notion of
circuit complexity.
For the standard robust notion of circuit complexity where
larger approximation errors are allowed, prior work was only
able to show a scaling that is worse than linear. It was shown in
[19] (see also Brandão, Chemissany, Hunter-Jones, Kueng, and
Preskill [2]) that the circuit complexity of a unitary drawn from
a constant multiplicative-error unitary t-design is Ω(t) with
high probability for t ≤ 2Θ(n) (see [12, Section 6]), implying
that the circuit complexity of random quantum circuits with L
gates must be at least Ω(L1/11 / poly(n)); the exponent 1/11
can be improved using [21]. In addition, Oszmaniec, Kotowski,
Horodecki, and Hunter-Jones [41] studied the long-time behavior of complexity, showing that complexity saturates at
maximal value after exponential time and undergoes recurrences after double exponential time, for both random quantum
circuits and stochastic local Hamiltonian evolution. This was
also conjectured in [1].
Complexity growth is a most natural question for random
circuits: a long random circuit is just a composition of some
random circuit and some additional random gates. If the first
random circuit part was already similar to Haar random and
had some amount of complexity, it is natural to ask how much
this complexity grows as we add additional gates to generate
the long random circuit. Even though the notion of complexity
“growth” is less natural for structured ensembles where one
does not simply add extra random gates, one may wonder whether the O(t)-depth structured t-design constructions
from [3], [36] provide some sequence of unitaries with linearly
increasing complexity as we increase the parameter t. Such a
statement does not follow directly from our analysis due to the
difference between additive and multiplicative errors; see [12,
Remark 6.4] for a detailed discussion.

The spectral gap of a distribution of unitaries is defined in
Eq. (1); see also [12, Section 2.1] for more details. Here, we
give the formal statements of our bounds on the spectral gap
of random reversible and quantum circuits (Theorem 1 and
Theorem 4), as well as the consequences of these bounds,
including: (1) random quantum circuits with Õ(n2 t) gates
form t-designs; and (2) a robust version of the Brown–
Susskind conjecture, which says that the complexity of random
quantum circuits grows linearly for an exponentially long time.
We remark that all the constants in this paper can (in principle)
be estimated explicitly.
1) Random reversible circuits: A random reversible circuit
on n bits consists of a sequence of elementary gates acting
on 3 bits. Each gate is sampled randomly and independently as follows: pick a uniformly random permutation from
Sym(23 ) and apply it to 3 randomly selected bits of the
input string.3 This procedure can be viewed as a random
walk, with each step being a randomly sampled gate from
the aforementioned distribution denoted as νrev,All→All . Our
main result on reversible circuits is the following theorem
comparing νrev,All→All to the uniform measure on Alt(2n )
(denoted by µ(Alt(2n ))), establishing a t-independent spectral
gap of Ω(n−3 ).

Brickwork circuits are a natural model for quantum devices
with 1D locality constraints on the qubits, so we will usually
state our main results for this model of random quantum

proof is to replace the qubit permutation with a sequence of
SWAP gates drawn uniformly at random, corresponding to
the connectivity of qubits. We then analyze this process using
some well-known results on the eigenvalues of Cayley graphs
on the symmetric group generated by transpositions.

C. Proof overview
In this section, we give a high-level overview of our spectral
gap proof. As noted above, one of the main implications of our

by a circuit of 3-bit reversible gates unless one uses an ancilla bit.

1311

spectral gap result is the linear growth of circuit complexity
(Theorem 8); we do not cover this implication here and instead
refer to [12, Section 6] and in particular [12, Remark 6.4].
As we remarked at the beginning of the introduction, a
key conceptual insight of our work is the use of structured
ensembles of permutations/unitaries to prove spectral gaps
for (structureless) random circuits. For both permutations and
unitaries, prior work has constructed structured ensembles with
good mixing properties ( [3], [4], explained below), but these
ensembles look a priori unrelated to random circuits. Our core
technical contribution is to connect these structured ensembles
to random circuits in a way that preserves mixing properties,
ultimately allowing us to show spectral gaps for both classical
and quantum random circuits.
At a high level, this happens in two steps: first, we show
that the structured ensembles have some efficient circuit implementation; this yields an ensemble of highly structured
(classical or quantum) circuits with good mixing properties.
The second step is to remove the structure from these circuits
until they become random circuits where each gate is chosen
independently and uniformly; our proof achieves this through
a carefully designed sequence of intermediate ensembles that
successively remove structure while preserving the mixing
properties.
Below, we sketch some of the key steps in our proof; the
full proof requires many steps, each with technical ideas, and
we refer to [12, Sections 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1] for more detailed
technical overviews.
a) Spectral gap for random reversible circuits: For
permutations, the structured ensemble that we start from is
a constant-sized set of generators for the alternating group
Alt((23s − 1)6 ) whose Cayley graph is expanding; this means
that the distribution that picks a generator uniformly at random
is spectrally gapped. (We will often abbreviate this by saying
that the generators are spectrally gappped.) Such a generating
set was constructed by Kassabov [4].
We face two obvious problems: First, Kassabov derived
his generators from an intricate algebraic construction, not
in terms of circuits; it is therefore unclear whether these
generators have any efficient circuit implementation (and given
that most permutations do not have efficient circuits, it may
seem unlikely that this would be the case). Second, Kassabov’s
generators generate the group Alt((23s − 1)6 ), but we are
interested in permutations on n bits, i.e., the group Alt(2n ).
We address the first problem by a detailed analysis of
Kassabov’s construction, which reveals that his generators do
have efficient circuits; indeed, we introduce a modification to
the construction from [4] that allows us to construct generators
with circuits that act on each bit only a constant number of
times. The constructed circuits act on n bits, but Kassabov’s
result works only for Alt((23s − 1)6 ); this means that there
is a (23s − 1)6 -sized “good subset” G of the 2n possible
input strings on which our circuits act as spectrally gapped
generators of permutations, but we need to extend the circuits
so that they form gapped generators for all of Alt(2n ), i.e., on
the whole set of 2n input strings. This is surprisingly subtle:

first, we modify our circuits so that they act as identity on
inputs outside of the good subset G. Then we use multiple
different embeddings of Alt((23s − 1)6 ) into Alt(2n ), each of
which gives rise to a different set of circuits with a different
“good subset” of inputs. Finally, we show that these different
embeddings can be combined to produce an ensemble of n-bit
circuits that forms a gapped generating set for Alt(2n ).
The second step is to relate these structured circuits to
random circuits with uniformly chosen gates. It is intuitively
plausible that this transformation should preserve the spectral
gap: replacing the gates in the structured circuit by uniformly
random gates appears to only add additional randomness that
should help the mixing properties. Formalizing this intuition
requires additional technical tools: we use Kazhdan constants,
a different way to characterize mixing properties, which obey
a very useful “short product formula” [12, Lemma 2.16], combined with an operator inequality between moment operators
that shows that uniformly sampling from a subgroup can only
yield a smaller spectral gap than sampling from the full group.
Together, these steps prove Theorem 1.
Converting from Theorem 1 to Theorem 2 is relatively
simple for unitaries [19], [24], but turns out to be much more
difficult for classical permutations: the quantum analysis uses
that the commutant of the representation U 7→ U ⊗t has a basis
with a useful approximate orthogonality property [25]. The
commutant of the representation π 7→ π ⊗t of the alternating
is more complicated and has no analogous property. The
key technical difficulty is analyzing how well a sequence
of random permutations acting on linear-sized overlapping
subsets of the bits of the input approximates a global random
permutation on the whole input. We prove a strong permutation overlap lemma by building on a polynomial interpolation
techniques for random matrices [36] (see [12, Section A]).
b) Spectral gap for random quantum circuits: For unitaries, the structured ensemble that we start from is the PFC
ensemble from [3]: the product of a uniformly random permutation matrix, a uniform binary phase (diagonal matrix with
±1-entries), and a uniformly random Clifford unitary. This
may not seem like a promising start. A random permutation
and a random binary phase cannot be implemented efficiently.
To pass to the structured ensemble that we started from in
the permutation case, there are no efficient circuits for the
PFC ensemble that we can try to relate to random circuits
with uniformly chosen gates. Our approach will therefore be
as follows: replace each of P, F, and C by steps of a random
walk on the corresponding subgroup (permutation, diagonal
phases, and Cliffords) of the unitaries, and use [3] to argue
that these subgroup walks combine to form a spectrally gapped
walk on the unitary group.
The first obstacle in this approach is that [3] only proved
that the PFC ensemble is an additive error design, whereas we
require spectrally gapped ensembles of unitaries. We show that
under certain conditions on the ensemble, the noncommutative
Riesz-Thorin theorem combined with the duality properties
of channel norms allows us to convert from additive errors
to spectral gaps. To apply this to the PFC ensemble, we

1312

have to modify it slightly, yielding the CPFPC ensemble
(product of uniform and independent Clifford, permutation,
binary phase, permutation, and Clifford), which we show is
spectrally gapped.
We now want to replace each component of the CPFPC
ensemble by a spectrally gapped walk on the corresponding
subgroup. However, this is not possible for binary phases,
which form an Abelian subgroup and therefore do not admit
a constant-sized set of generators with a spectral gap [46]. We
therefore replace the binary phase by P̃ (σZ ⊗ I)P̃ −1 , where
P̃ is a uniformly random permutation and σZ the single-qubit
Pauli-Z matrix. This is similar to a binary phase except that
the number of +1 and −1 entries are the same; we show that
this makes no difference for the spectral gap. The matrices
P̃ (σZ ⊗ I)P̃ −1 may look unpleasant (they do not form a
group and use the same permutation twice in sequence), but
they become easy to deal with when inserted into the CPFPC
ensemble: the random permutations surrounding the binary
phase F in CPFPC absorb the permutation P̃ and we get
the CPZPC ensemble, where Z stands for σZ ⊗ I and all
components are independent.
We can now replace the random Cliffords and the random
permutations by randomly chosen elements from a spectrally
gapped set of generators for the Clifford and permutation
groups. For Cliffords, such generators with O(n)-sized circuit
implementations are easy to construct because the Clifford
group is relatively small. For the permutation group, we
use random circuits, leveraging Theorem 1. The result is an
ensemble of efficient structured circuits with the spectral gap
property.
The final step is to relate these structured circuits to uniformly random ones while preserving the spectral gap. Classically, we used Kazhdan constants as a key tool, but this relied
on our ensemble of structured circuits to be constant-sized.
Quantumly, our structured circuit ensemble has exponentially
many elements, which would result in an exponential loss
when converting from Kazhdan constants to spectral gaps. We
therefore use a different argument: we first show that we can
write modify our structured ensemble into a convolution of
distributions that sample uniformly from local subgroups; this
relies on the properties of the random circuits we inserted for
our permutations and Clifford in the previous step. This local
subgroup structure allows us to use tools from frustration-free
Hamiltonians to formalize the intuition that sampling from a
random circuit with uniform gates can only introduce more
randomness than sampling from local subgroups, proving the
spectral gap for all-to-all connected quantum circuits.
To show a similar spectral gap for brickwork quantum
circuits, we interpret an all-to-all random quantum circuit
(where gate locations are chosen at random) as a brickwork
quantum circuit interleaved with a random permutation of
the qubit order after each gate; this random permutation
effectively randomizes the gate locations that were fixed
in the brickwork circuit. We then approximate the random
qubit permutation with SWAP gates and relate the resulting
circuit back to uniform random quantum circuits using the

Hamiltonian complexity tools mentioned above. This strategy
generalizes and allows us to relate random quantum circuits
on arbitrary connected architectures to each other.
D. Discussion and outlook
In this work we prove near optimal gaps of Ω̃(1/n) for
the t-th moment operator of random reversible circuits for
t ≤ Θ(2n/6.1 ) and random quantum circuits for t ≤ Θ(22n/5 ).
This is proven for all-to-all random reversible classical circuits
and both all-to-all and brickwork random quantum circuits.
We also remark that our overlap theorem [12, Theorem A.1]
can likely be used together with the martingale technique for
spectral gaps of frustration-free Hamiltonians [20] to prove
a spectral gap of Ω̃(1/n) for random reversible circuits in a
1D brickwork layout, improving upon the Ω̃(1/t) spectral gap
in [16] for brickwork reversible circuits. This spectral gap estimate implies approximate unitary t-designs and approximate
t-wise independent permutations after Õ(n2 t) gates.
As a consequence, we show that the robust quantum circuit
complexity grows at a linear rate for an exponentially long
time, which was conjectured by Brown and Susskind [1],
[2]. Moreover, we prove an analogous statement for random
reversible circuits, showing that random circuits are effectively
incompressible with overwhelming probability. Our gap estimate for random quantum circuits also improves bounds on
the mixing time of other random processes on the unitary
group such as the dynamic of stochastic Hamiltonians [28].
Moreover, the fast convergence to designs allows us to improve
predictions about random quantum circuits that involve strong
concentration properties [47]. For example, our designs bounds
together with the results of [48] show that the fluctuations
of the entropy S(ρA (d)) decay super-exponentially fast in
the depth, where A ⊂ [n] with |A| = O(1) and ρA =
Tr[n]\A [|ψ⟩⟨ψ|], where |ψ⟩ = Ud · · · U1 |0n ⟩ is generated by
random quantum circuits of d gates. More precisely, we find
Pr[S(ρA (d)) ≤ |A| − δ] ≤ (e2δ d · 2−n )d/ poly(n)
While our spectral gap estimates n−1 /polylog(n, t) are
optimal up to polylog factors (see, e.g., the discussion in [49]),
there are multiple avenues for future work. In particular, it
would be desirable to lift the assumption t ≤ Θ(2n/2 ). We
use this condition many times and it is precisely the regime in
which the permutations are approximately orthogonal [25]. In
this regime, a t×t submatrix behaves approximately Gaussian,
so that the t-th moments cannot see the correlations between
Haar random matrix entries. We cannot rule out that this
condition is fundamental to the 1/ poly(n)-gap. On the other
hand, it was suggested that the gap might be 1/ poly(n) for
all t ≥ 1 in [19], which is the quantum version of the result
we have proven for random reversible circuits.
A more ambitious open problem regards the precise value of
the gap for random quantum circuits. Numerically, the gap for
large t appears to be equal to the gap for t = 2. In other words,
additional irreps of SU(2n ) beyond those already appearing
